title: Gregory the Great (540–604)
hook: he calls himself servant of the servants of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columba of Iona, a peregrinus, the pilgrim for Christ who built a monastery at the edge of the map. Your line was the island.

Servant of the servants of God. That's what one bishop of Rome called himself in his letters. He was a monk who didn't want the job. His name was Gregory. He came from a wealthy Roman family, gave his life to prayer, and founded a monastery in the city itself. He's the same Gregory who wrote down Benedict's life. Then Rome's bishop died, and the people of Rome chose Gregory.
screen: `SERVANT OF SERVANTS.` → `A MONK WHO DIDN'T WANT IT.` → `ROME CHOOSES GREGORY.`

segments.voice: Pope is what Catholics call the bishop of Rome, whom they understand as the successor of Saint Peter and the shepherd of the whole Church. Start with Gregory's reluctance. Gregory of Tours, in his History of the Franks, says Gregory tried to escape it, even writing to the emperor asking him not to approve the choice. It didn't work; he was made bishop of Rome anyway. Next, what he did with it. Rome was battered by flood and plague. Gregory of Tours describes him calling the whole city out to pray, walking in processions through the streets while the sickness went on. He kept writing letters, which still survive, to bishops, rulers and ordinary people. He also wrote a book on how a pastor should live, calling the care of souls the art of arts. Now the title. When the bishop of Constantinople used the title universal bishop, Gregory objected in his letters: that title, he said, was too proud for any bishop. For himself, he kept using another: servant of the servants of God. It echoes something Jesus tells his disciples in the Gospels: whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all. Gregory took that teaching and made it his name. Catholics believe the pope has real authority. Gregory's point is about how it's held. A servant of servants is at the bottom of the ladder, serving the very people who serve. In Gregory's hands, the office Catholics see as the highest in the Church described itself from the lowest place. Catholics call him Saint Gregory the Great, pope and Doctor of the Church.
screen: `THE BISHOP OF ROME.` · `HE TRIED TO ESCAPE IT.` · `PLAGUE, PRAYER, THE ART OF ARTS.` · `A TITLE FROM THE LOWEST PLACE.` · then, large: `SERVANT OF SERVANTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who serve you without much notice, the driver of your bus, the person who cleans your office, a cashier, a nurse, a parent who cooks, and pick one. Hold that person in mind for a moment and ask what they carry that you never see, and what a real thank you, using their name, might mean to them. If you pray, pray for them.
Pope. The bishop of Rome, whom Catholics understand as Peter's successor. Gregory held the office and called himself servant of the servants of God. Today's word.
Your line: servant of servants. In Gregory's hands, greatness looked like service. That's day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great, and popes still use the title servant of the servants of God in solemn documents.

chat.says: Why did Pope Gregory call himself servant of the servants of God?
options: He had real authority but took Jesus's words to heart: the first must serve all.
His critics forced the title on him to mock his refusal to be pope.
He was apologizing for being too strict with the monks who served him.

notes: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 10.1: Gregory from a senatorial family, founded monasteries, chosen by the people after Pelagius died in plague, wrote to the emperor asking him not to consent; flood and plague in Rome. Paraphrased; confirm.

Pastoral Rule 1.1: 'ars est artium regimen animarum'. Confirm.
